---
title: "Predicting Spatial Classes with Random Forest"
date: 2026-09-11
categories: [tool, geoml, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre: upload a labeled point file (or use the built-in example), train a Random Forest on it, turn labeled points into a full classification surface, measure on held-out points how much that surface is worth, and see a real gotcha where R silently swaps classification for regression."
---

A few labeled points on their own only answer questions about
themselves: "what class is point #7?" is a question you can already
answer by looking at the file. The useful question is the one you
*can't* already answer: "what's the likely class everywhere else,
including where I have no data at all?" A Random Forest trained on
labeled points, then applied to a regular grid across the whole area,
turns a sparse set of samples into a full classification surface, the
same shift in usefulness a sparse rain-gauge network gets from
interpolating a rainfall map between the gauges.

Whether that surface is worth trusting is a separate question, and one
this article measures rather than assumes: a quarter of the points is
held out of training and used only for scoring.

A `.geojson`, or a shapefile (either as a single `.zip`, or as
`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together): see the upload section
below.

Just want to classify a file with adjustable settings, any class
column, and a download button, without the rest of the reading? Use
the [standalone tool](/tools/spatial-classifier.html) — same engine,
less prose.

## 1. Why the coordinate system matters here

A Random Forest trained directly on longitude/latitude would treat 1
degree of separation as the same "distance" everywhere on Earth, which
it isn't. Both languages below pick a working UTM zone from the data's
own bounding-box center and reproject into it first, same reasoning,
same formula, as this site's [Viewshed](raster-viewshed.qmd) and
[Spatial Clustering](spatial-clustering.qmd) tools: a reasonable
default for one local dataset, not a universally correct choice for
points spanning multiple UTM zones or very large areas.

No file uploaded, or your file has no column literally named
`class`? Both cells below fall back to the same built-in survey: 150
points across three zones (`south`, `centre`, `north`) whose
boundaries undulate rather than running straight, plus deliberate
label noise — one point in nine carries the wrong class, standing in
for the labelling error a real survey has. Both tabs build it from the
same arithmetic rule instead of a list of coordinates, so the points
are identical and the two languages are comparable.

That noise is there on purpose. Two tidy, well-separated clusters
would let any classifier score a perfect 100%, which teaches nothing
except misplaced confidence. Number of trees and grid resolution are
fixed here (100 trees, a 10-cell grid) to keep the focus off tuning;
the [standalone tool](/tools/spatial-classifier.html) exposes both as
adjustable controls and lets you pick any column as the class.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classification-py}
#| package: geopandas, scikit-learn
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

# The example survey, used only when nothing was uploaded (or the
# upload has no `class` column). Written as a rule rather than a list
# of coordinates, so the structure is visible instead of buried in 150
# pairs of numbers: points on an irregular lattice, three bands whose
# boundaries undulate across the area, and deliberate label noise.
# Integer arithmetic only (no random numbers, no trigonometry), so the
# R tab further down builds exactly the same points.
FALLBACK_NEXT_CLASS = {"south": "centre", "centre": "north", "north": "south"}

def fallback_points():
    points = []
    for i in range(150):
        col, row = i % 15, i // 15
        lon = 12.4450 + col * 0.0010 + ((i * 37) % 11 - 5) / 10000
        lat = 41.8850 + row * 0.0012 + ((i * 53) % 13 - 6) / 12000
        # Triangular wave on the column index: the two band boundaries
        # rise and fall across the area instead of running straight, so
        # no single horizontal cut separates the classes.
        tri = abs((col * 2) % 8 - 4) - 2
        cls = "south" if row < 3 + tri else ("centre" if row < 6 + tri else "north")
        # One point in nine is relabelled to the next class: a stand-in
        # for the labelling error a real survey carries. It is what
        # keeps the held-out accuracy below a meaningless 1.00.
        if i % 9 == 0:
            cls = FALLBACK_NEXT_CLASS[cls]
        points.append(((lon, lat), cls))
    return points

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
if gdf is not None and gdf.crs is None:
    gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
    crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
elif gdf is not None and str(gdf.crs) != "EPSG:4326":
    gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

if gdf is None or "class" not in gdf.columns:
    fallback = fallback_points()
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        {"class": [cls for _, cls in fallback]},
        geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
            [pt[0] for pt, _ in fallback],
            [pt[1] for pt, _ in fallback]
        ),
        crs="EPSG:4326"
    )
    crs_warning = None

labeled = gdf[gdf["class"].notna()].copy()
labeled["class"] = labeled["class"].astype(str)

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone

labeled_proj = labeled.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
proj_x = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
proj_y = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()

# A single UTM zone distorts badly, to the point of returning inf,
# for points far enough from it. Dropped here rather than failing:
# nothing in this article compares points by position across
# languages, so partial exclusion doesn't desync anything.
finite_mask = np.isfinite(proj_x) & np.isfinite(proj_y)
labeled_proj = labeled_proj[finite_mask]
X = np.column_stack([proj_x[finite_mask], proj_y[finite_mask]])
y = labeled_proj["class"].values

if len(y) == 0:
    raise ValueError(
        f"None of the labeled points could be projected into a single UTM "
        f"zone (EPSG:{calc_epsg}) -- this dataset spans too wide an area "
        "for this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more "
        "local file."
    )

class_labels = sorted(set(y.tolist()))

# A quarter of the points is held out and never shown to the model, so
# the accuracy below is measured on points it has not already seen.
# stratify=y keeps each class's share the same on both sides of the
# split: without it a rare class can end up entirely in one half.
# Skipped when there is too little to split -- an uploaded file can
# have a class with a single member, and holding that one out would
# leave the class untrained. "No accuracy" is then reported as exactly
# that, rather than as a score of 0.
class_counts = {c: int((y == c).sum()) for c in class_labels}
can_split = len(class_labels) >= 2 and min(class_counts.values()) >= 2 and len(y) >= 10

if can_split:
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0
    )
else:
    X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = X, y, None, None

# X is (x, y) coordinates only: position is the ONLY predictor here.
# This demonstrates how a Random Forest turns labeled points into a
# surface, not a general land-cover classifier. Real covariates
# (spectral bands, elevation, soil type) would change what the model
# is actually learning.
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

accuracy = None
class_accuracy = {}
if X_test is not None:
    predicted_test = model.predict(X_test)
    accuracy = round(float((predicted_test == y_test).mean()), 3)
    # Per class as well: one overall number can hide a model that is
    # perfect on the largest class and useless on another.
    for c in class_labels:
        in_class = y_test == c
        if in_class.sum() > 0:
            class_accuracy[c] = round(float((predicted_test[in_class] == y_test[in_class]).mean()), 3)

# Regular 10x10-ish square-cell grid over the full extent, at a fixed
# resolution: keeps the focus on how the two languages disagree,
# rather than on tuning parameters.
gdf_proj = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
full_x = gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
full_y = gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()
full_finite_mask = np.isfinite(full_x) & np.isfinite(full_y)
gminx, gmaxx = float(full_x[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_x[full_finite_mask].max())
gminy, gmaxy = float(full_y[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_y[full_finite_mask].max())
width, height = gmaxx - gminx, gmaxy - gminy
cell_size = max(width, height, 1e-6) / 10
n_cols = max(1, int(np.ceil(width / cell_size)))
n_rows = max(1, int(np.ceil(height / cell_size)))

centers_x, centers_y = [], []
for row in range(n_rows):
    for col in range(n_cols):
        centers_x.append(gminx + (col + 0.5) * cell_size)
        centers_y.append(gminy + (row + 0.5) * cell_size)
centers = np.column_stack([centers_x, centers_y])
predicted = model.predict(centers)

half = cell_size / 2
cells = [
    Polygon([
        (cx - half, cy - half), (cx + half, cy - half),
        (cx + half, cy + half), (cx - half, cy + half),
        (cx - half, cy - half)
    ])
    for cx, cy in centers
]
grid_wgs84 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"predictedClass": predicted}, geometry=cells, crs=calc_epsg
).to_crs("EPSG:4326")
training_wgs84 = labeled[["class", "geometry"]]

{
    "trainingFeatures": training_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "gridFeatures": grid_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "classLabels": class_labels,
    "labeledCount": int(len(labeled)),
    "trainCount": int(len(y_train)),
    "testCount": int(len(y_test)) if y_test is not None else 0,
    "accuracy": accuracy,
    "classAccuracy": class_accuracy,
    "gridCellCount": int(len(cells)),
    "crsWarning": crs_warning
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-classification-r}
#| package: sf, randomForest, geojsonsf, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(geojsonsf)
library(randomForest)

# The same example survey the Python tab builds, from the same rule:
# 150 points on an irregular lattice, three bands with undulating
# boundaries, one point in nine relabelled to stand in for survey
# error. Integer arithmetic only, so both languages produce identical
# points -- which is what makes the two tabs comparable at all.
fallback_points <- function() {
  i <- 0:149
  col <- i %% 15
  row <- i %/% 15
  lon <- 12.4450 + col * 0.0010 + ((i * 37) %% 11 - 5) / 10000
  lat <- 41.8850 + row * 0.0012 + ((i * 53) %% 13 - 6) / 12000
  tri <- abs((col * 2) %% 8 - 4) - 2
  cls <- ifelse(row < 3 + tri, "south", ifelse(row < 6 + tri, "centre", "north"))
  next_class <- c(south = "centre", centre = "north", north = "south")
  flip <- i %% 9 == 0
  cls[flip] <- unname(next_class[cls[flip]])
  data.frame(lon = lon, lat = lat, class = cls, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (!is.null(data) && is.na(st_crs(data))) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!is.null(data) && !isTRUE(st_crs(data) == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}

if (is.null(data) || !("class" %in% names(data))) {
  data <- st_as_sf(fallback_points(), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
  crs_warning <- NULL
}

labeled <- data[!is.na(data$class), ]
# The one step that decides classification vs. regression -- see
# section 5 below. Without this, randomForest() below would silently
# fit a REGRESSION on `class` instead.
labeled$class <- factor(as.character(labeled$class))

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
bnd <- st_bbox(data)
center_lon <- (bnd[["xmin"]] + bnd[["xmax"]]) / 2
center_lat <- (bnd[["ymin"]] + bnd[["ymax"]]) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone

labeled_proj <- st_transform(labeled, calc_epsg)
coords_train <- st_coordinates(labeled_proj)

# A single UTM zone can map far-away points to infinity. Dropped
# here rather than failing outright: this article never compares
# points by position across languages, so partial exclusion doesn't
# desync anything.
finite_rows <- is.finite(coords_train[, 1]) & is.finite(coords_train[, 2])
if (!any(finite_rows)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "None of the labeled points could be projected into a single UTM zone ",
    "(EPSG:", calc_epsg, ") -- this dataset spans too wide an area for ",
    "this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more local file."
  ))
}
coords_train <- coords_train[finite_rows, , drop = FALSE]
labeled_proj <- labeled_proj[finite_rows, ]

all_df <- data.frame(x = coords_train[, 1], y = coords_train[, 2], class = labeled_proj$class)

# Both the holdout below and the forest itself draw random numbers, so
# without a seed two runs of this cell give different answers. The
# Python tab passes random_state=0 for the same reason.
set.seed(0)

# A quarter of the points held out, sampled separately within each
# class so every class keeps its share on both sides -- base R has no
# stratified-split function, but split() + sample() is the whole idea.
# Skipped when there is too little to split (an uploaded file can have
# a class with a single member, and holding that one out would leave
# the class untrained).
class_counts <- table(all_df$class)
can_split <- length(class_counts) >= 2 && min(class_counts) >= 2 && nrow(all_df) >= 10

if (can_split) {
  test_idx <- unlist(lapply(
    split(seq_len(nrow(all_df)), all_df$class),
    function(idx) sample(idx, max(1, round(0.25 * length(idx))))
  ))
  train_df <- all_df[-test_idx, ]
  test_df <- all_df[test_idx, ]
} else {
  train_df <- all_df
  test_df <- NULL
}

# Position is the ONLY predictor here (class ~ x + y): this
# demonstrates how a Random Forest turns labeled points into a
# surface, not a general land-cover classifier. Real covariates
# (spectral bands, elevation, soil type) would change what the model
# is actually learning.
model <- randomForest(class ~ x + y, data = train_df, ntree = 100)

# Accuracy on the held-out quarter, overall and per class: one overall
# number can hide a model that is perfect on the largest class and
# useless on another.
accuracy <- NULL
class_accuracy <- NULL
if (!is.null(test_df)) {
  predicted_test <- predict(model, newdata = test_df)
  accuracy <- round(mean(predicted_test == test_df$class), 3)
  per_class <- lapply(levels(all_df$class), function(cl) {
    in_class <- test_df$class == cl
    if (any(in_class)) {
      jsonlite::unbox(round(mean(predicted_test[in_class] == test_df$class[in_class]), 3))
    } else {
      NULL
    }
  })
  names(per_class) <- levels(all_df$class)
  class_accuracy <- per_class[!vapply(per_class, is.null, logical(1))]
}

# The prediction surface: a regular grid covering the full extent, at
# the same fixed resolution the Python tab uses, so the two results
# are directly comparable. st_make_grid() builds it from an origin, a
# cell size and a cell count in one call.
coords_all <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(st_transform(data, calc_epsg))))
finite_all <- is.finite(coords_all[, 1]) & is.finite(coords_all[, 2])
gminx <- min(coords_all[finite_all, 1])
gmaxx <- max(coords_all[finite_all, 1])
gminy <- min(coords_all[finite_all, 2])
gmaxy <- max(coords_all[finite_all, 2])
cell_size <- max(gmaxx - gminx, gmaxy - gminy, 1e-6) / 10
n_cols <- max(1, ceiling((gmaxx - gminx) / cell_size))
n_rows <- max(1, ceiling((gmaxy - gminy) / cell_size))

grid <- st_make_grid(
  cellsize = cell_size,
  offset = c(gminx, gminy),
  n = c(n_cols, n_rows),
  crs = st_crs(calc_epsg)
)

# Each cell is classified by the point at its center: the model was
# trained on point coordinates, so that is the only thing it can be
# asked about.
grid_centers <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(grid))
predicted <- predict(model, newdata = data.frame(x = grid_centers[, 1], y = grid_centers[, 2]))

grid_wgs84 <- st_transform(
  st_sf(predictedClass = as.character(predicted), geometry = grid),
  4326
)
training_wgs84 <- st_sf(
  class = as.character(labeled$class),
  geometry = st_geometry(labeled)
)

result <- list(
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  classLabels = sort(levels(labeled_proj$class)),
  labeledCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(nrow(labeled))),
  trainCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(nrow(train_df))),
  testCount = jsonlite::unbox(if (is.null(test_df)) 0L else as.integer(nrow(test_df))),
  accuracy = if (is.null(accuracy)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(accuracy),
  classAccuracy = class_accuracy,
  gridCellCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(length(grid))),
  modelType = jsonlite::unbox(model$type),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning)
)
out <- jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)

# The two GeoJSON payloads are attached AFTER that round-trip, not
# inside it: sf_geojson() already returns finished JSON, and passing
# it through toJSON() a second time would turn every scalar inside it
# ("type": "Feature") back into a one-element array.
out$gridFeatures <- jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(grid_wgs84), simplifyVector = FALSE)
out$trainingFeatures <- jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(training_wgs84), simplifyVector = FALSE)
out
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Same palette/roles as the Spatial Classifier tool -- reused here
// rather than invented fresh, so a reader who's seen the tool
// recognizes the same visual language.
CLASS_PALETTE = ["#ab502b", "#42583c", "#3d5a73", "#c48a2e", "#8b2f24"]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Each language draws onto its own map sources, so running only one
// of them still produces a visible surface. The two grids cover the
// same extent at the same resolution, so where both have run the
// fills overlap -- which is the point: any cell the two languages
// classified differently shows up as a color that doesn't match.
classPaint = (classLabels, field, opts = {}) => {
  const expr = ["match", ["get", field]];
  classLabels.forEach((label, i) => {
    expr.push(label, CLASS_PALETTE[i % CLASS_PALETTE.length]);
  });
  expr.push("#766851");
  if (opts.fill) {
    return { "fill-color": expr, "fill-opacity": 0.45, "fill-outline-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0)" };
  }
  return {
    "circle-color": expr,
    "circle-radius": 6,
    "circle-stroke-width": 1.5,
    "circle-stroke-color": "#2a2117"
  };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

pyResult = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("spatial-classification-py", Generators)
{
  if (pyResult) {
    await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("spatial-classification-grid", pyResult.gridFeatures, {
      paint: classPaint(pyResult.classLabels, "predictedClass", { fill: true })
    });
    await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("spatial-classification-training", pyResult.trainingFeatures, {
      paint: classPaint(pyResult.classLabels, "class")
    });
    await sharedMap.fitToData(pyResult.gridFeatures);
    mutable pySummary = pyResult;
    mutable crsWarning = pyResult.crsWarning;
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Same "two cards side by side, seeing them agree IS the point"
// reasoning as this site's CRS Mismatch and Spatial Clustering
// articles.
statCard = (label, s) => {
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.style.flex = "1";
  wrap.style.minWidth = "260px";

  const heading = document.createElement("div");
  heading.className = "webgeods-label";
  heading.textContent = label;
  wrap.appendChild(heading);

  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  wrap.appendChild(box);

  const row = (rowLabel, value) => {
    const dt = document.createElement("div");
    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = rowLabel;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };

  if (!s) {
    row("Calculation CRS", "—");
    return wrap;
  }

  row("Calculation CRS", s.calculationCrs);
  row("Classes", s.classLabels.join(", "));
  row("Labeled points", s.labeledCount);
  if (s.accuracy === null || s.accuracy === undefined) {
    // Not a score of 0: there were too few points to hold any out.
    row("Held-out accuracy", "too few points to hold any out");
  } else {
    row("Held-out accuracy", `${s.accuracy} (${s.testCount} of ${s.labeledCount} points held out)`);
    row("By class", Object.entries(s.classAccuracy ?? {}).map(([k, v]) => `${k} ${v}`).join(" · "));
  }
  row("Grid cells predicted", s.gridCellCount);

  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
statCardsRow = {
  const row = document.createElement("div");
  row.style.display = "flex";
  row.style.flexWrap = "wrap";
  row.style.gap = "16px";
  row.append(statCard("Python", pySummary), statCard("R", rSummary));
  return row;
}
```

${resetMapButton}

The filled grid is the predicted surface; the dots on top are the
labeled training points, colored the same way. Each language draws
onto its own map sources, so running either one on its own is enough
to see a result.

Run both and the two surfaces won't match everywhere. They cover
exactly the same ground and start from identical points (the two cells
build the survey from the same arithmetic rule), but they don't label
every cell the same way. It's tempting to read that as Python
disagreeing with R. It isn't: both cells fix a seed so their output is
reproducible, and changing that number moves the surface just as much
as switching language does. A forest retrained disagrees with itself
about as much as the two languages disagree with each other.

## 4. How good is that surface?

The stat cards answer that, and the answer is sobering. A quarter of
the points is held out of training and used only for scoring, so the
accuracy is measured on points the model has never seen — and on the
built-in survey it lands around **0.63**, against 0.33 for guessing at
random among three classes.

The per-class row matters more than the overall one. The outer `north`
band scores about 0.87, while `centre` — the middle band, squeezed
between the other two and undulating across the area — gets between a
third and a half of its held-out points right, depending on which
quarter was held out. One overall number would have hidden that
completely: the model has essentially learned two of the three classes.
That's the case for reporting accuracy per class whenever the classes
aren't interchangeable, which spatially they rarely are.

Two cautions before reading much into any of these numbers.

**The number itself moves.** Across five seeds the accuracy spanned
roughly 0.53–0.68 in Python and 0.63–0.74 in R: overlapping ranges, so
five runs are nowhere near enough to claim one implementation beats the
other. The two tabs also hold out *different* points, because their
random number generators differ — another reason a gap between the two
accuracies says nothing about scikit-learn versus randomForest.

**And it flatters the model.** This is the specifically spatial catch.
Nearby points are correlated, so a randomly chosen test point almost
always has a training point a few metres away, and the model can lean
on that neighbour instead of generalising. A random holdout on spatial
data is therefore optimistic: 0.63 is closer to an upper bound than to
an honest estimate. The standard answer is spatial cross-validation,
which holds out whole *blocks* of area rather than scattered points, so
the test data sits somewhere the model genuinely hasn't seen. That is a
subject of its own; what matters here is knowing the number is
generous, not conservative.

The two cautions are the same fact seen twice. The surface is supported
where the points are and guessing where they thin out, and a score
computed from points sitting right next to the training data measures
the supported part while telling you nothing about the rest.

## 5. A silent switch: classification vs. regression

The disagreements above are a model being unsure. This one is
different: a model quietly solving a different problem.

scikit-learn's `RandomForestClassifier` and R's general-purpose
`randomForest()` decide what to do very differently. scikit-learn is
unambiguous: you asked for a *Classifier*, so it classifies,
whatever the labels look like. R's `randomForest()` instead looks at
the *type* of the target column, and the two ways of getting this
wrong fail very differently:

- A plain **character** column (`"north"`/`"south"`, never wrapped in
  `factor()`) fails loudly. R can't compute a regression mean on
  text, so the fit errors out immediately with something like
  `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Annoying, but safe: you
  find out right away.
- A column of **numbers standing in for classes** (`0`/`1`, or a
  status code read straight out of a file) is the dangerous one: it
  fits without complaint and silently runs a **regression** instead of
  a classification. No error, no warning, just a different kind of
  model whose predictions no longer look like class labels at all.

The R cell above already does this correctly (`factor(as.character(...))`
before the fit): `modelType` in its stat card reads `classification`.
Here's the realistic failure case: the exact same points, with `class`
read in as `0`/`1` instead of `"north"`/`"south"` (exactly what
happens if a class column arrives as a numeric status code), and that
one `factor()` step skipped, run live:

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-classification-r-nofactor}
#| package: sf, randomForest, jsonlite
library(randomForest)

# The same survey as the cell above, built from the same rule.
i <- 0:149
col <- i %% 15
row <- i %/% 15
lon <- 12.4450 + col * 0.0010 + ((i * 37) %% 11 - 5) / 10000
lat <- 41.8850 + row * 0.0012 + ((i * 53) %% 13 - 6) / 12000
tri <- abs((col * 2) %% 8 - 4) - 2
cls <- ifelse(row < 3 + tri, "south", ifelse(row < 6 + tri, "centre", "north"))
next_class <- c(south = "centre", centre = "north", north = "south")
flip <- i %% 9 == 0
cls[flip] <- unname(next_class[cls[flip]])

# The one difference: `class` arrives as a NUMERIC status code
# (0 = south, 1 = centre, 2 = north) and is NOT wrapped in factor(),
# unlike the cell above. A character column here would error
# immediately (see the prose above); a numeric one fits silently.
class_code <- c(south = 0, centre = 1, north = 2)[cls]

train_df <- data.frame(x = lon, y = lat, class = unname(class_code))
model <- randomForest(class ~ x + y, data = train_df, ntree = 100)

result <- list(
  modelType = jsonlite::unbox(model$type),
  sampleTrueClass = jsonlite::unbox(train_df$class[1]),
  samplePrediction = jsonlite::unbox(as.numeric(predict(model, train_df[1, ])))
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
mutable noFactorResult = null
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
noFactorRaw = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("spatial-classification-r-nofactor", Generators)
{
  if (noFactorRaw) mutable noFactorResult = noFactorRaw;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
noFactorCard = {
  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  const row = (label, value) => {
    const dt = document.createElement("div");
    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = label;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };
  if (!noFactorResult) {
    row("model$type", "—");
    return box;
  }
  row("model$type", noFactorResult.modelType);
  row(`predict() on a point labeled ${noFactorResult.sampleTrueClass}`, noFactorResult.samplePrediction.toFixed(3));
  return box;
}
```

${noFactorCard}

`model$type` reads `regression`, and `predict()` on a point whose true
class was `0` ("north") returns a number like `0.1` or `-0.05`, not
the class `0` itself, a *regression estimate* that happens to land
near it. Nothing in the output says a switch happened; the only way to
notice is checking `model$type` yourself, which is exactly what
production code should do.

::: {.callout-note}
This is real, verified behavior of `randomForest()`, run live on this
page, not an edge case invented for the article: the R cell in
section 3 above does the correct `factor()` coercion, one line
different from the cell above. scikit-learn's separate `Classifier`/
`Regressor` classes make the same mistake structurally impossible: the
class you instantiate *is* the decision, made once, up front.
:::
